subject: Chemistry
title: Wave-Particle Duality
description: Learn Wave-Particle Duality in one minute.

hook.text: Electrons behave as particles when you detect them and as waves when you don't. They're both and neither.

buildup.text: In 1924, Louis de Broglie proposed that all matter has wave properties. The smaller the particle, the larger the wave.

discovery.text: The double-slit experiment proved it: electrons fired one at a time build up an interference pattern—like waves.

twist.text: But if you watch which slit each electron goes through, the wave pattern vanishes. Observation changes behavior.

climax.text: This duality is fundamental. Electron microscopes work because electron wavelengths are smaller than light—revealing atoms.

punchline.text: Particle or wave depends on how you look. Reality is stranger than intuition.

quiz.question: What happens when you observe which slit an electron passes through?
options: The wave interference pattern vanishes and electrons behave like particles
The electron splits into two halves

details.summary: Wave-particle duality is the quantum mechanical principle that particles like electrons exhibit both wave-like and particle-like behaviors depending on how they are observed. Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924 that all matter has wavelength, and experiments confirmed this for electrons in 1927.
details.whyItMatters: Duality explains diffraction, interference, and the structure of electron orbitals. It fundamentally changed our understanding of what matter is at the smallest scales.
takeaways: Electrons behave as waves in some experiments and particles in others
De Broglie proposed all matter has an associated wavelength
The double-slit experiment dramatically demonstrates duality

faq.question: How can something be both a wave and a particle simultaneously?
faq.answer: It is not literally both at the same time. Rather, quantum objects have properties that manifest differently depending on the experiment. When you look for particle-like collisions, you find them. When you design wave-like interference tests, you see interference patterns.

faq.question: Do large objects like humans have a de Broglie wavelength?
faq.answer: Yes, but the wavelength is vanishingly small. A walking human has a de Broglie wavelength of roughly 10^-35 meters, far smaller than any atom. Wave effects are only observable for objects with extremely small mass, like electrons or neutrons.
